items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I was playing there with a trio and in the summer they cut down and said can you just come in with two guitars and make it easy? And John did it with me

ctx.x: What was his attitude toward what you do? Did he realize how much playing you had done up to that point?

Well he knew, but I think it set in when we played one summer together at the Pierre Hotel. I was playing there with a trio and in the summer they cut down and said can you just come in with two guitars and make it easy? And John did it with me and then he got his baptism of fire there with me giving him the dirty looks when he hit the wrong chord. And he gave them to me when I did. But fortunately he can sit down with a tune and come up with a good set of chords for it. That’s what I like about him.

items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 23, 2003 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I know John is about to make an album. He does a lot of research on it. I used to tell him listen to this guy, listen to that guy.

ctx.x: Your kids have done well for themselves. I’m wondering if you’ve gotten to the point where you learn anything from them?

Oh yeah. Yeah. They come up with some good stuff. Tunes — I know John is about to make an album. He does a lot of research on it. I used to tell him listen to this guy, listen to that guy. He does a great rendition of a certain tune you ought to look into. That’s all. That’s as far as it goes. But he’s got a hot trio. They’re very good.
Yeah. He’s got a good personality on stage.

items.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: It’s like with Bucky I knew when his eyebrows went up, okay he’s going to either turn it over to me or here comes the shout chorus or something of that, that was the message.

ctx.x: I just, that’s so interesting. And I’ve seen it. I’ve probably done it myself, but the look, like you get this look and with guitar players, you know there’s the hand, and the look should tell you what this is going to be. And you go, “Well that could be lot of things.”

Yeah. But since we’ve been playing together they know that that means they know what the section is. It’s like with Bucky I knew when his eyebrows went up, okay he’s going to either turn it over to me or here comes the shout chorus or something of that, that was the message. I know that there’s a couple of things, somebody wrote the other day, it was Ray Brown’s birthday and somebody wrote — oh George Fludas the drummer put up a thing that was Ray, George Fludas and Larry Fuller at the piano and Fludas had gone…
Was there such a thing in a jazz group as like five sharps, or jazz guys don’t play in five sharps, but rock guys do.

items.title: Ruth & Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Saddle River, New Jersey, January 19, 2015
items.q: So we used him on a record date, John and I.

ctx.x: I don’t know, he gave me the impression that you helped him not get in trouble.

Yeah, well, in other words, when I heard him play on a ship he was playing in a jam session one night. I said, “who the hell is that drummer?” It was Pretty Purdie. And he was swinging. So we used him on a record date, John and I. He played “Sing Sing Sing” — it was unbelievable. He knew it backwards.
All right, I’m going to try another tune on you here. I’m just going to give you —
